Placing Points

In videogames and computer graphics, we often want to distribute something throughout a space, like placing trees in a videogame forest or points to sample in a raytracer. In cases like these, the most straightforward approaches have some big drawbacks. If we simply choose points in a regular grid, it will look artificial and produce aliasing effects and Moiré patterns. If we avoid those effects by choosing positions of the points independently using random numbers, we will tend to have the problem of too much clustering of points and large gaps between clusters of points. We need a balance between the chaos of pure randomness and the unnatural order of regular spacing, keeping the points looking evenly spaced when viewed at large scales, but not quite predictable when we consider a zoomed-in view. Distributions meeting those criteria are sometimes called blue noise.

250 Points distributed on a uniform grid 250 Points distributed randomly Blue noise (250 points)

Colors of Noise

The term "blue noise" comes from signal processing used in the electronics and audio fields. It is sort of making an analogy with visible light to characterize noisy signals based on how much different frequencies are contributing to it. In audio, we experience this as the pitch and timbre of a sound, and in light we perceive it as color. White noise is probably the most familiar "color of noise". It is so named because, like white light, it is made up of a balance of many different frequencies. When the light we see contains more of the higher frequencies of light, we percieve it as blue light. So blue noise is noise that favors higher frequences. If we want to get technical, the colors of noise are defined in terms of power spectral density.

White noise (top) and its relatively flat power spectrum (bottom) Blue noise (top) and its power spectrum (bottom) which favors higher frequencies Brownian noise AKA red noise (top) and its power spectrum (bottom) which favors lower frequencies

If it seems a little odd to think of frequencies and power spectra when you are trying to plant some virtual plants, you could think of it this way: low-frequency noise would mean that large areas of the image look different from each other, and high frequency noise would mean that when you zoom in, a small area of the image looks different from another small area. Like white light, white noise is varied at all scales. Blue noise, like blue light, favors higher frequencies, giving us the properties we want: no particular part of the space as a whole looks favored, but exact placements are unpredictable and uncorrelated.

To efficiently come up with our own evenly-spaced-but-random points, we'll use a technique called Fast Poisson Disk Sampling, which I believe comes from a SIGGRAPH paper by Robert Bridson. The defining property of a Poisson disk sampling is that the points are distributed with no two closer together than some chosen minimum distance. At a high level, Bridson's algorithm works by first picking a random seed point, then for future points, it steps at least a minimum distance away in a random direction and tests to see if that new point is not too close to one we already have. This is made efficient by linking points to an underlying grid that lets us quickly determine which points could be near the candidate point.

The Algorithm

Inputs to the Algorithm

Our fast Poisson disk function will do its thing based on: the size of the area/volume to place things in, a minimum distance between the generated points, a maximum number of points to generate, and an additional tunable number, max_tries, that will make more sense later, but essentially controls how hard it works to fill the space around a generated point before it gives up on placing more near it. 30 is a typical value.

Bridson's algorithm works in any number of dimensions, but I am presenting it here in only two dimensions for simplicity's sake.
